extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism and philosophy; writers interested in evaluating mystical, religious, or philosophical prose
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative observations for judging mystical, theological, and philosophical prose (contrast between 'learned' literati and unlearned mystics), as found in a literary-biographical critical essay. Emphasises qualities like depth, immediacy, symbolism, and the relation of style to substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fullness of heart and intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a work may be measured by the 'fulness of heart and intellect' it contains — even a single simple page may surpass whole folios in depth and worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts that there exist 'folios on the human understanding' which would 'have a far juster claim to their high rank and celebrity, if in the whole huge volume there could be found as much fulness of heart and intellect, as burst forth in many a simple page' of mystics like George Fox or Jacob Behmen. Anti-pattern: long learned volumes lacking heartfelt substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and immediacy of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlearned or 'simple' authors often express thought as 'immediate echoes' of feeling; simplicity of soul gives immediacy and emotional authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such writers use a small stock of images/language (e.g., the Bible as 'sole armory') and formulaic phrases ('It was discovered unto me', 'I could not forbear'), which should be read as signs of immediate feeling rather than mere rhetorical affectation. Evaluate such writing by emotional sincerity and immediacy rather than polished rhetorical technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style versus substance (orthography and smooth periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical polish — correct orthography and smooth period-making — should not be conflated with depth or truthfulness of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts 'the haughty priests of learning' who 'could write orthographically, make smooth periods, and had the fashions of authorship at command' with genuine inspiration. Anti-pattern: valuing a writer primarily for rhetorical smoothness while overlooking lack of heart or originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality, depth, compression, and solidity of distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical works are judged by originality, depth, compression of thought, novelty, subtlety yet solidity of distinctions, and the logical strength of argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant is praised for 'originality, the depth, and the compression of the thoughts; the novelty and subtlety, yet solidity and importance of the distinctions; and the adamantine chain of the logic.' Evaluate philosophical prose on these intellectual qualities and on clarity/evidence where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and evidence (where attainable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and evident argumentation are virtues; even dense philosophy can and should exhibit clearness and evidence to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Critique is lauded for 'the clearness and evidence' of its reasoning. Where obscurity remains, it should be defensible (hints, insinuations) rather than gratuitous confusion. Scoring note: balance value for depth with penalty for unnecessary obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbol for highest ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Highest or most profound ideas often must be conveyed symbolically; symbolism is a legitimate and necessary mode for certain concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay states: 'An idea, in the highest sense of that word, cannot be conveyed but by a symbol; and, except in geometry, all symbols of necessity involve an apparent contradiction.' Readers should expect symbolic/hieratic modes in attempts to convey transcendent ideas and judge whether the symbol communicates rather than merely obscures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity/equivocation as deliberate protective strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity, mythic or equivocal expression may be used deliberately by authors to avoid personal danger or social/political persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that 'Questions which cannot be fitly answered without exposing the respondent to personal danger' may justify 'express[ion] either mythically or equivocally.' When evaluating such texts, consider whether obscurity is protective and purposeful rather than mere opacity or incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity as intention to communicate truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Veracity in philosophical/religious writing is measured not only by literal statements but by the writer's intention to communicate truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: 'Veracity does not consist in saying, but in the intention of communicating, truth.' Thus a measured, symbolic, or partial statement may be truthful in intent even if not exhaustively literal. Evaluate honesty of purpose alongside literal accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to keep 'heart in the head' and prevent dogmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable writings maintain a balance between feeling and intellect, preventing the mind from being imprisoned within a single dogmatic system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mystics 'contributed to keep alive the heart in the head' and 'prevented [the author] from being imprisoned within the outline of any single dogmatic system.' Reward works that sustain emotional life within intellectual inquiry and that encourage openness rather than doctrinal confinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of penetration versus learned caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine penetration to 'the inmost centre' of things may come from unlearned or non-professional inquirers, because professional literati often tacitly limit speculative inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay observes a 'secret and tacit compact among the learned, not to pass beyond a certain limit in speculative science,' leaving deeper inquiry to the 'illiterate and the simple.' In evaluation, consider whether work shows brave penetration beyond fashionable limits versus cautious conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's responsibility: bringing superior spirit and judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writings (especially mystical) require the reader to bring 'a spirit and judgment superior to that of the writers' to derive intelligible meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that 'in order to derive any advantage ... the reader must bring with him a spirit and judgment superior to that of the writers themselves.' Thus part of evaluating such works is diagnosing whether their obscurities demand readerly resources rather than indicating authorial failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional/physiological signs not to be taken as literal metaphysics
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong bodily or nervous sensations and imaginative spectres in inspired authors may be symptoms of intense inner experience rather than literal metaphysical revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat from the text: 'the man's body should sympathize with the struggles of his mind; or that he should ... mistake the tumultuous sensations of his nerves ... as parts or symbols of the truths which were opening on him.' Evaluate mystical testimony with sensitivity to psychological/physiological origins; distinguish symbol from claimed external fact.
